newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OSCE urges Belgrade -- "Respect poll results".
newsitem.headline: OSCE urges Belgrade -- "Respect poll results".

text.p: Europe's security forum said on Thursday a solution to the political crisis in Belgrade was simple.

The government of Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic had to recognise fully the opposition victories in local elections last November and quickly hand over seats on town councils, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) said.
Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen of Denmark, which took over the OSCE chairmanship on January 1, said he had made these points clear in a letter to Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic.

"The OSCE has made its stand absolutely crystal clear. The municipal elections of November should be respected," Petersen told a news conference after addressing the Vienna-based OSCE permanent council.

"Instead of seemingly giving concessions as the government (of Yugoslavia) is doing, the situation is much more simple -- they need to abide by the results of the elections...and give seats to the people who won the election," he added.

Tens of thousands of people have demonstrated daily for almost nine weeks in a bid to reinstate victories by the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition annulled by the ruling Socialists, who claimed unspecified "irregularities".
Serbian electoral commissions conceded on Tuesday that the ruling leftists had lost Belgrade and the second city Nis.

Two weeks ago, the OSCE council backed a report by former Spanish premier Felipe Gonzalez who had visited Serbia on behalf of the organisation to study the disputed local polls and had found that the opposition had indeed won the polls. The report called on Belgrade to respect the results.
In his letter to Milutinovic, Petersen said Gonzalez had based his report on initial voting results and that these results could not be a subject for discussion or negotiation.

Petersen advised Belgrade in his letter to make legal changes "to prevent the distortions now possible through various means, including invalidating the vote on minor technical pretexts and ordering new votes in a seemingly arbitrary manner". Reuters obtained the letter through diplomatic sources.

Petersen told the permanent council earlier that he was willing to open talks with Belgrade on ways to improve democracy in the country in such fields as freedom of the media, an independent judiciary and improvements to the electoral system.
"Democratisation is the name of the game. The government of Serbia must start the process of democratisation," he said.
Asked whether the OSCE position was encouraging the opposition to make further demands beyond the reinstatement of the election results, Petersen said:
"It is absurd to talk about (the OSCE) intervening in any illegal way in the internal matters of others. But it is the "raison d'etre' of the OSCE to intervene in favour of democratisation."

He said talks on the local elections had to be kept separate from any discussion of Yugoslavia's re-admittance to the 54-member OSCE. Belgrade was suspended in 1992 after being accused of stoking the war in neighbouring Bosnia.
Among other issues, Petersen said Belgrade had to accept the return of OSCE missions to the Serbian regions of Kosovo, Sandjak and Vojvodina.
